overview: This Arakan record spans 1783 to 1878: the kingdom’s final years, Burmese conquest in 1784 to 1785, and British rule from 1826. It represents a region under changing governments. Its unchanged outline hides these political transitions and should not be treated as a precise administrative boundary.

periods.title: Burmese provincial rule
periods.summary: Governors, garrisons and resistance replaced the independent court.

periods.title: Early British administration
periods.summary: The Treaty of Yandabo transferred Arakan to British control.

periods.title: A division of British Burma
periods.summary: Arakan joined a combined colonial province.

sections.title: Conquest, displacement and a new colonial government

items.text: After the Burmese conquest, Arakan’s king, members of his family, officials and other captives were taken across the mountains. The revered Mahamuni Buddha image was also removed to the Burmese royal heartland. Losing a court meant more than changing the name on a map: households were uprooted, and an important center of religious devotion was carried away.

Resistance continued under Burmese provincial government. Revolts, forced labor and flight brought Arakanese refugees across the frontier into British-controlled Bengal. This created disputes over people as well as territory. The frontier was a place where families tried to find safety while rulers argued over who could cross it and who should be returned.

The Treaty of Yandabo, signed on 24 February 1826 after the First Anglo-Burmese War, named Arakan, Ramree, Cheduba and Sandoway as territories retained by the British. Its third article made the Arakan Mountains the frontier with Burma. The atlas keeps the same regional shape across this change, although the governing power had changed decisively.

In 1862, the colonial government combined Arakan, Pegu and Tenasserim within British Burma. Each division had its own commissioner under a chief commissioner. This was administrative integration within Britain’s Indian empire, not the restoration of Arakan’s independent monarchy. The surviving orders let us trace how officials reorganized a region after conquering it.

sections.title: Families, rice and the port market

items.text: Buchanan’s 1798 journey describes Arakanese refugees around Ramu, across the frontier in Bengal. Nearby households grew tobacco, chilies and betel leaf around their huts; farmers also planted sugar for their own use. These observations belong to the borderland where displaced families were rebuilding lives, not to a survey of every household remaining in Arakan.

By 1849, Akyab, now Sittwe, shipped rice to distant markets. Nuthall’s trading memorandum explains why ships had to respect the monsoon: grain needed sun-drying before husking, while cleaned rice kept poorly in the damp climate. Much was prepared only when needed. A ship arriving too early could spend an expensive visit waiting for the weather.

Different rice varieties ripened in succession, with harvesting running from late November into February. Loading was especially favorable in February, March and April. Farmers, grain cleaners, brokers and sailors therefore worked to connected seasonal timetables. Sending a bag of rice overseas involved a chain of tasks long before it reached a ship’s hold.

Nuthall said fish, meat, bread and vegetables could generally be bought in Akyab’s market. For imports he listed soap, umbrellas, crockery, sugar and many sorts of cloth, advising merchants to choose especially bright printed fabrics. The shopping list is a colorful glimpse of demand at the port, though it does not show what every family could afford.

The rice business also involved bargaining power. Furnivall’s economic history describes Akyab millers using advances to press sellers for lower prices in the early 1870s. A later attempt to hold prices down broke when one firm bought aggressively. Farmers’ earnings depended partly on buyers, credit and shipping arrangements, not simply on how much rice they grew.

sections.title: Learning, health and the labor behind town improvements

items.text: Akyab’s government school, established in 1846, became a high school in 1875. A report from Maungdaw describes parents seeking English lessons so their children could obtain clerical jobs. Enrollment revived after a teacher arrived from Akyab. This particular school dispute shows families weighing education against the opportunities offered by the colonial economy.

The late-1870s district account describes Akyab’s hospital and dispensary as raised buildings connected by a covered passage. Europeans and local patients occupied separate blocks. The buildings show organized medical provision, but also the unequal categories of colonial society. Their existence does not tell us how easily all families could obtain treatment.

Roads, drains and filled swamps required considerable work. The district account states that prisoners performed much of it; their tasks also included rope-making, weaving bags, carpentry and smithing. Timber-sawing was introduced in 1875. Town improvements depended partly on coerced labor, so a tidy street could conceal a much less comfortable story about who built it.

sections.title: Shrines, women’s patronage and a recorded language

items.text: An 1876 account of Akyab’s Buddermokan shrine, preserved by archaeologist Emanuel Forchhammer, records masonry buildings, a rock-cut retreat and a local foundation legend involving traders whose turmeric became gold. The miraculous cargo is a story people told, not an established event. Recording both structures and traditions helps us understand what a sacred place meant to its visitors.

That account also preserves a woman’s contribution: Mah Ming Oung received permission to build at Buddermokan in 1849 and had its water tank re-dug. Custodianship later passed within Hussain Ally’s family, eventually to his daughter Me Moorazamal. The record brings women, family responsibilities and practical maintenance into the history of a religious site.

A small language sample appears in Buchanan’s 1799 vocabulary: “Bel” means “sun”, “Tara” means “stars”, and “Pannæ” means “water” in the column labeled Rooinga. He attributed this speech to Muslim communities long settled in Arakan. These are a collector’s printed Roman transcriptions, preserved in a scholarly reprint, rather than native-script writing or a modern spelling standard. They represent one of the region’s languages, not everyone’s speech.

ending.text: Nothing ended Arakan’s communities or colonial administration in 1878. That year closes this imported map record. Arakan continued within British Burma, while its inhabitants maintained and reshaped their households, religious institutions and livelihoods under colonial rule. The loss of independent kingship belonged to 1784 to 1785, and the transfer to British rule to 1826.
